passage:
I'm Jyoti, and Ankita has been my best friend since first year. She's the most talented illustrator in our design batch, and this year she has turned down everything. The college magazine cover: "Not good enough yet." The children's book project with a real publisher: "Maybe next year." The group show: she didn't even reply.
I can't read her mind, but whenever someone praises her old work, she looks almost pained.
Last month I tried something different. I brought my own sketchbook, the messy one, full of crossed-out hands and wonky faces, and showed her page after page. "This is how mine start," I said. She laughed at a horse that looked like a sofa.
Then I stopped saying "your work is amazing" and started saying things like "you tried a new brush today" or "that's further than yesterday."
On Friday she sent me a rough sketch for the magazine. Just a rough one. I didn't make a fuss.

qa.q: What did one of Jyoti's sketches look like, according to Ankita's laugh?
qa.a: A horse that looked like a sofa.

qa.q: Why might Ankita look almost pained when her old work is praised?
qa.a: Praise for results may feel like a standard she must keep meeting, so it adds to her fear of making something less than perfect.

qa.q: Which of Jyoti's changes helped Ankita, and why?
qa.a: Showing Jyoti's own messy sketchbook and praising effort and progress instead of results made imperfect work feel normal and safer to share.

qa.q: What might it have meant for Ankita to see Jyoti's crossed-out hands and wonky faces?
qa.a: It may have shown Ankita that even good artists start messily, easing her belief that only perfect work can be seen.

grounding: Shows a friend who notices a talented illustrator turning down chances, and helps by sharing her own messy sketches and praising effort and progress.

passage:
Monday, first week of term. Dr Deepika Rao noticed that Trisha, the sharpest student in her economics seminar, had not submitted the optional essay again, and had quietly declined the research assistant post Deepika offered. "I'm not ready," Trisha said, eyes down.
Thursday, two weeks later. Deepika tried something she had never done in class. She put her own first draft of a journal paper on the projector, red notes and all, including a paragraph she had rewritten six times. "This is what my work looks like before it's good," she said. The class laughed. Trisha leaned forward.
Friday, a month later. Trisha handed in a messy two-page draft with a note: "Not finished." Deepika wrote back only about what she had tried: "Bold argument in section two. Good progress from your first idea."
The next week Trisha asked whether the assistant post was still open.

qa.q: What did Deepika put on the projector?
qa.a: Her own first draft of a journal paper, red notes and all.

qa.q: What does Trisha's 'I'm not ready', said with eyes down, suggest?
qa.a: It suggests fear of producing less than perfect work rather than a lack of ability.

qa.q: Which of Deepika's responses helped loosen Trisha's grip, and why?
qa.a: Showing her own flawed draft and commenting on effort and progress rather than polish made imperfect work feel safe to hand in.

qa.q: How might Trisha have felt seeing the lecturer's red-marked draft?
qa.a: Trisha may have felt surprised and relieved that even an expert's writing starts rough, which is why she leaned forward.

grounding: Illustrates a lecturer who sees a strong student declining chances, and helps by showing her own messy draft and praising effort and progress.

passage:
Gautam, you ask why I keep my old lesson plans with red corrections all over them? Let me tell you about a student I had, back when I taught college English and everyone called me Bhavna ma'am.
Her name was Nandita. Brilliant. But she turned down the essay competition, the magazine, the debate. "I'm not ready, ma'am." She hardly submitted anything.
One day I did something I'd never done. I showed her my own first draft of a published article, full of crossings-out, arrows, a whole paragraph deleted. She stared. "Yours, ma'am?"
After that, whenever she handed in anything, I praised the effort and the progress, not only the result. By the end of the year she'd entered the competition. She didn't win. But she entered.

qa.q: What did Bhavna show Nandita?
qa.a: Her own first draft of a published article, full of crossings-out.

qa.q: What was Bhavna probably feeling as she watched Nandita turn down chance after chance?
qa.a: She was likely frustrated and concerned, seeing strong ability going unused out of fear.

qa.q: In the story, which choice helped Nandita change?
qa.a: Showing her own messy draft and praising effort and progress, not only results.

qa.q: What was it like for Nandita to see the messy draft?
qa.a: Nandita seemed surprised and perhaps relieved, seeing that even her teacher's good work started imperfect.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how showing her own flawed draft and praising effort helped a talented student stop turning down chances.

The hackathon registration closed in an hour, and the canteen Wi-Fi kept dropping. Chetan pushed his laptop towards Minakshi. "Register. Please. You're the best coder I know."
"I'm not ready. My projects aren't polished."
"You said that about the internship too. And the coding contest."
Minakshi shrugged.
Chetan hesitated, then opened his own project folder. "Look at this. My first app. It crashed every five minutes. My code is a mess." He scrolled through ugly lines. "I still entered last year. I learned more than all semester."
Minakshi stared at the screen. "It really crashed?"
"Constantly. Register. I'll team with you."
She reached for the laptop.

qa.q: How long until hackathon registration closed?
qa.a: An hour.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when he pushed his laptop towards Minakshi?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and eager, sad to see her talent going unused out of fear.

qa.q: What did Chetan do that helped Minakshi?
qa.a: He showed his own messy, crashing first app and offered to team up, making imperfection feel normal.

qa.q: What is it like for Minakshi to see Chetan's messy code?
qa.a: Minakshi seems surprised and a little relieved, seeing that even good coders start with flawed work.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing strong ability unused and chances turned down, and helping by sharing his own flawed work.

Damini had taught Pema in the Darjeeling college for two years. Pema's essays, when she submitted them, were among the best in the class. But she'd turned down the state essay prize, the student journal and a research assistant role. "Not ready, ma'am."
Damini stopped praising only her marks. Instead she said things like, "I liked how you tried a new argument here." And one day she brought her own draft of a conference paper, full of red corrections from her supervisor.
"You get corrected too?"
"All the time. That's how it gets good."
Next week, Pema asked for the journal submission form. Her hand shook as she took it.

qa.q: What did Damini bring to show Pema?
qa.a: Her own conference paper draft, full of red corrections.

qa.q: What might Damini have felt as Pema turned down opportunity after opportunity?
qa.a: She was likely concerned and a little sad, seeing strong ability going unused out of fear.

qa.q: Which of Damini's changes helped loosen the fear?
qa.a: Praising Pema's effort and new ideas rather than only marks, and showing her own corrected draft.

qa.q: What is Pema feeling when she takes the form with a shaking hand?
qa.a: Pema feels nervous but brave, taking a chance despite the fear.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing strong ability going unused and helping by praising effort and sharing her own corrected draft.

"Nandini, the photography club wants you for the exhibition. They asked me to ask you."
"No. My photos aren't ready."
"You said that about the college magazine too. And my cousin's wedding shoot."
"Because they weren't ready." Nandini pulled her sleeves over her hands. "People will look closely."
Gargi opened her laptop. "Look at this. My exhibition statement. First draft."
Nandini leaned in. "There's a typo in line one. And this sentence doesn't even end."
"Yep. I sent it to the club anyway, and they helped me fix it. Here's version three." Gargi scrolled. "Still not perfect."
Nandini was quiet. "You just sent the messy one?"
"I sent the messy one. And I've noticed you've been shooting at the lake every evening for a month. That's real work, even if nobody has seen it."
"Maybe one photo," Nandini said. "The heron one."

qa.q: Which photo did Nandini finally offer?
qa.a: The heron one.

qa.q: Why did Gargi show Nandini her own messy first draft?
qa.a: Gargi was concerned to see Nandini's talent going unused and hoped an imperfect draft would ease Nandini's fear.

qa.q: What in Gargi's approach helps loosen Nandini's grip on perfection?
qa.a: Gargi shows a flawed draft and praises the month of evening practice, valuing effort and progress, not only finished results.

qa.q: What is the exhibition invitation like for Nandini?
qa.a: It feels frightening, since people will look closely, and she pulls her sleeves over her hands before agreeing to one photo.

grounding: Shows a friend seeing strong ability unused and chances refused, and helping by sharing flawed drafts and praising effort and progress.
